title: YouTube as a source of information on the non-pharmacological treatment of COPD
screen_reason: Cross-sectional analysis of the 97 most-viewed YouTube videos on non-pharmacological COPD treatment (searched 5 December 2024). Each video was classified useful, misleading or neither against the GOLD report and clinical COPD guidelines, with 'misleading' defined as containing at least one scientifically incorrect or unsubstantiated claim: 13 of 97 (13.4%) were misleading. Items judged for truth against an external ground truth and reported as a share = CONTENT. The mDISCERN, JAMA and GQS scores are QUALITY and are reported only as medians, so they generate no row.

estimates.country: not stated; videos in English, Danish, Norwegian or Swedish, no geographic restriction
estimates.date: searched 5 December 2024 (videos of any upload date; median 2,046 days since upload)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-viewed YouTube videos on non-pharmacological COPD treatment classified as misleading
estimates.denominator: 97 YouTube videos with more than 30,000 views, in English, Danish, Norwegian or Swedish, with non-pharmacological COPD content, retrieved from the first three pages of most-viewed results for three search terms
estimates.definition: Video classified 'misleading' when it contained at least one scientifically incorrect or unsubstantiated claim regarding the epidemiology, diagnosis, non-pharmacological treatment, symptoms, risk factors or treatment of COPD
estimates.misinfo_def: "misleading" (Containing at least one scientifically incorrect or unsub­ stantiated claim regarding the epidemiology, diagnosis, nonpharmacological treatment, symptoms, risk factors, or treatment of COPD)
estimates.source_quote: Of the 97 videos, 83 (86%) were categorized as useful, 13 (13%) as misleading, and 1 (1%) as neither.
estimates.page_loc: Results p. 3 and Table 2; also Abstract and Conclusion
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent reviewers assessed each video; scientific accuracy was judged against the GOLD report and clinical COPD guidelines, falling back on meta-analyses where guidelines were silent; discrepancies were reviewed independently and disagreements resolved by senior researchers. No kappa or other agreement statistic is reported, and the authors state that the usefulness categorisation is not a validated gold standard and that their own nutrition and exercise expertise may have made them stricter on those topics.
estimates.moderator_quote: Searches were sorted by "most viewed". Previous research has shown that people rarely load more than the first three pages [29].
estimates.notes: denom_selection=curated: the sample is rank-truncated (most-viewed sort, first three pages) and view-thresholded at 30,000, which the authors name as a selection-bias limitation. Coded CONTENT rather than QUALITY because the misleading label requires a scientifically incorrect or unsubstantiated claim checked against GOLD, so a wholly accurate video cannot receive it; the mDISCERN, JAMA and GQS instruments used alongside are quality tools and are reported only as medians. The Methods sentence reads 'the cut-off of <30,000 views ... were included', which contradicts the Abstract's '>30,000 views'; the abstract reading is the sensible one. QUOTE NOTE: value_pct 13.4 and the 85.6/1.1 figures in value_raw are Table 2's own percentages, but this text file dumps Table 2 as a scrambled column list, so no contiguous span pairs the label 'Misleading' with '13 (13.4%)'; source_quote is therefore the Results sentence, which states the count and denominator verbatim (13 of 97, rounded there to 13%). 13/97 = 13.4% exactly, so the value is an R8-legal part/whole share. The definition quote carries the file's soft-hyphen artifact ('unsub- stantiated').

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons. (1) '62% of the misleading videos contained misinformation on the nutritional management of COPD' (Abstract) and 'nutrition-related content was dominant among the misleading videos, accounting for 61% of them' (Discussion): a topic composition computed inside the 13-video misleading set, not a falsity share, and the two statements of it disagree (62% vs 61%; 8/13 = 61.5%). (2) '85% of all misleading videos were uploaded by healthcare professionals' - composition of the misleading set, not a prevalence. (3) Misleading rates by uploader type from Table 2 (MD 10.5%, non-MD HCP 27.6%, non-HCP 14.3%, association 7.1%, company 50%, news and entertainment 25%, university or hospital 0%, specialist 0%): these are the paper's secondary headline ('non-MD HCP sources were the most misleading') and could justify subgroup rows, but several cells are tiny (company n=2, specialist n=1, news n=4) and the overall row already carries the estimate, so I left them out. (4) Comment analysis of the 13 misleading videos (260 comments: 70% agreement, 16% follow-up questions, 10% correction/debunking, 4% commercial or spam, 1% not relevant) measures audience response inside an all-misinformation set, not prevalence. (5) mDISCERN (useful 3 vs misleading 1), JAMA (3 vs 2) and GQS (3 vs 3) are reported as medians with IQRs only; per the instructions a scale reported only as a central tendency yields no row. (6) Topic frequencies (symptoms 77%, diagnosis 48%, lectures 25%, smoking cessation 24%) describe content coverage, not accuracy. (7) Engagement comparisons (views, subscribers, likes, comments per day) are counts and medians, not shares. (8) 'a total of 41% of 2675 included medical videos contained misinformation' is quoted from Okagbue et al.'s review, not this study's data, so R8 forbids keeping it. (9) DATA-INTEGRITY FLAG: the screening arithmetic does not reconcile. The text says 229 videos were collected, of which 144 were duplicates and 2 unavailable, then 17 excluded for language before analysis and, during analysis, 16 more for language, 11 for pharmacological content and 1 off-topic; that leaves 38, not 97, while another sentence says '132 videos' were excluded from 229 to reach 97. The flowchart is an image so it could not be checked.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of YouTube. Three searches ('COPD', 'Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease', 'Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease') run in incognito mode on 5 December 2024, sorted by most viewed, at least three result pages per search; inclusion required more than 30,000 views, English or Scandinavian language, and non-pharmacological content, giving 97 videos after removing duplicates and exclusions. Two independent reviewers classified each video as useful, misleading or neither against the GOLD report and clinical guidelines, and scored modified DISCERN, JAMA benchmark criteria and the Global Quality Score; disagreements were resolved by senior researchers. No inter-rater reliability coefficient is reported. Non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U, median test) on engagement. Author-stated limitations: selection bias from the view threshold and language restriction, a snapshot design on a dynamic platform, instruments not developed for video, unavoidable subjectivity in scoring, the usefulness categorisation not being a validated gold standard, and possible evaluator bias because both primary authors specialise in nutrition and physical activity, the domains where most misleading content was found. One senior author declares honoraria and a research grant from pharmaceutical companies unrelated to the study. The screening counts in the Results do not add up to the 97 included videos.
